title: The Default-Off Classroom: Redefining 1:1 Programs for Meaningful Learning
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek argues that schools answer parental worries about 1:1 laptops with plumbing, such as filters and acceptable use policies, when they should explain the learning. He says the root problem is that the technology director and the head of school rarely share a clear picture of what devices exist, what they can reach, and when they are open. Screen time, he claims, is an empty data set because minutes with a lid open say nothing about purpose, and he cites the latest PISA findings that moderate, subject-guided device use goes with stronger performance. His remedy is a default-off classroom in which lids stay closed until a teacher names a purpose, built through a shared baseline statement, a joint walkthrough of two dozen classrooms, and a few professional learning hours. He previews his book The School Leaders Guide to Digital Wellness and a companion guide, and ends with a two-sentence test every adult on campus should be able to answer.
points: Schools explain the logistics of a 1:1 program well and the learning poorly, and families notice the gap.
The technology director and school head must jointly own three facts: what devices students have, what those devices can reach, and when they are open.
Counting screen minutes measures nothing; the useful data is the reason a lid was opened and whether that purpose was met.
Default off is presented as a baseline rather than a retreat, and the proposed rollout is a baseline statement, an identical walkthrough count in September and January, and a handful of PD hours.
quotes: We are very good at explaining the logistics of a 1:1 program and very poor at explaining the learning, and families can tell the difference.
Walk into any 1:1 school and ask four people the same three questions: how is technology used here, why do students have devices, and at what age do they get them.

Screen time is an empty data set. A count of minutes with a device open cannot say what happened in those minutes, and the way it gets reported quietly supplies the answer anyway: every minute was the tool being used as intended.
When the lid is closed until a teacher opens it, the minutes stop being the question. The reason it was opened is the question, and whether the purpose was met is the data.
A school device is a tool among tools. Sometimes it is the right one. Sometimes the right tool is a pencil, a printed novel, a lab bench, a walk outside, or two students talking to each other.
People stay where you put them. The lid-up classroom is a default nobody chose, set by a cart, a login, and a pandemic. Resetting it is a decision, and it has to be made by two people at once.
It sounds straightforward: students receive laptops in middle school when academic tasks demand them, and those screens remain down until an educator specifies a clear purpose.
